units.name: command-core
units.role: Defines a CLI command tree and drives its execution lifecycle.
units.description: This is the heart of the Cobra library: the definition of a 'Command', one node in a tree of CLI commands and subcommands, like 'git' and 'git commit', and the engine that runs it. It holds a command's name, help text, flags, and callback functions, lets a program author build up a tree of commands and subcommands, and drives the whole lifecycle of running a program: parsing the command line, finding which command was requested, running its before/after hooks and its main action, and printing help/usage/version text when needed. It also contains a handful of small shared helpers (a spell-check-style suggestion helper, template utilities, generic error-checking helpers) and a small Windows-specific guard that shows a friendly message if the program was double-clicked from Explorer instead of run from a terminal.

effects.description: CheckErr (cobra.go:238) and the Windows mousetrap guard (command_win.go:39) call os.Exit to terminate the process on error. Command output/input defaults to os.Stdout/os.Stderr/os.Stdin (command.go:393-410), and ExecuteC reads os.Args[1:] as the default argument list (command.go:1105-1106).

On Windows, preExecHook sleeps for MousetrapDisplayDuration via time.Sleep before exiting (command_win.go:34); it also blocks on fmt.Scanln() waiting for a keypress when the duration is 0, and calls mousetrap.StartedByExplorer() to detect an Explorer-launched process (command_win.go:31,37).

units.name: positional-args
units.role: Rules for how many positional (non-flag) arguments a command accepts.
units.description: This is the set of ready-made rules a command-line tool author can attach to a command to control how many plain (non-flag) words a user is allowed to type after the command name, and optionally restrict which words are acceptable. For example, a command can say 'I need exactly 2 arguments' or 'I need at least 1' or 'only these specific words are valid arguments,' and if the user doesn't comply, the tool automatically shows an error instead of running. It is a small, pure decision-making policy with no side effects of its own; it just inspects the arguments it's given and returns yes or no.

units.name: flag-groups
units.role: Declares and enforces business rules about relationships between a command's flags.
units.description: This code lets a command author declare rules about how a command's flags relate to each other: which flags must always be supplied together (e.g. --user and --pass), which sets require at least one flag to be picked (e.g. --json or --yaml), and which flags may never be used at the same time (e.g. --json and --yaml being mutually exclusive). When someone actually runs the command, this code checks the flags they typed against those declared rules and produces a clear error if they broke one. It also feeds the same rules into the shell's tab-completion system so that, as a user types, the shell can hint which flags are now required or should be hidden.

units.name: active-help
units.role: Builds and reads the environment-variable-driven configuration for Cobra's Active Help hints, and appends hint text into completion output.
units.description: This code implements Cobra's 'Active Help' feature: while a user is pressing tab to auto-complete a command in their shell, the program can show short contextual hint messages, like 'you must specify a name here,' alongside the normal list of completions. This unit provides the building block a program author uses to attach such a hint to the list of suggestions, plus the logic that figures out whether hints should be shown at all or silenced, based on an environment variable the end user or the program can set, either a global on/off switch for all Cobra-based programs, or a program-specific one.

units.name: completion-engine
units.role: Computes dynamic shell-completion suggestions at runtime and exposes the API for registering custom completion logic.
units.description: This is the brain of Cobra's shell tab-completion feature. When a user presses Tab while typing a command in bash/zsh/fish/PowerShell, the generated completion script invokes a hidden internal command; this unit figures out, given what the user has typed so far, what to suggest next: subcommand names, flag names, or flag values using completion logic the CLI author registered. It also defines the public API that CLI authors use to plug in their own completion behavior (registering per-flag completion functions, per-command 'valid args' functions, and options like disabling the auto-generated completion command), plus small debug-logging helpers for troubleshooting completion scripts.

units.name: shell-completion-scripts
units.role: Renders shell-specific completion script text (bash legacy/v2, zsh, fish, PowerShell) and writes it to a Writer or file; defines the bash annotation-key constants and the Mark* API for tagging flags.
units.description: This part of Cobra turns the tree of commands and flags a developer has defined into a ready-to-install script for a specific shell: bash, zsh, fish, or PowerShell. A user runs something like 'mytool completion bash' or calls the equivalent library function directly, and this code writes out a script that, once sourced or saved into the right place, makes pressing Tab in that shell smart about the program's commands and flags. It also provides a small set of 'Mark' functions that let a developer tag individual flags, for example 'this flag only accepts filenames' or 'this flag is required', so the generated scripts and the live completion engine can behave correctly for those flags.

units.name: docs-generator
units.role: Renders a built command tree as man pages, Markdown, ReStructuredText, or YAML reference documentation.
units.description: This package turns a program's command structure, all its subcommands, flags, and help text, into ready-to-read reference documentation. Given a fully built command tree, it can produce a UNIX man page, a Markdown page, a ReStructuredText page, or a YAML description for a single command, or walk the whole command tree and write one file per command into a directory. It handles formatting details like listing each command's flags, cross-linking parent and child commands under a 'SEE ALSO' section, and stamping each generated page with a creation date, so that tools built with this CLI framework can automatically ship accurate, navigable documentation alongside their code.

violations_observed.note: InitDefaultCompletionCmd (completion-engine) directly invokes the Gen*Completion methods of shell-completion-scripts to build the built-in 'completion' subcommand, while shell-completion-scripts also depends back on completion-engine's ShellCompDirective constants and active-help's activeHelpEnvVar/activeHelpMarker. The two units are mutually dependent rather than a clean one-way boundary; recorded as a finding rather than resolved by moving files, since InitDefaultCompletionCmd is otherwise cohesive with the rest of completions.go.

prepareCustomAnnotationsForFlags reads completion-engine's package-level flagCompletionFunctions map directly (via a shared mutex) instead of going through an exported accessor. This is a coupling to completion-engine's internal mutable state rather than a call to one of its declared entrypoints.

Command.ValidateArgs invokes whatever function is stored in the c.Args field (of type positional-args.PositionalArgs). Since Args is a pluggable field rather than a fixed function call, the edge is recorded against the PositionalArgs type itself; the actual function invoked at runtime is chosen by the command-core caller from positional-args' exported constructors (or a user-supplied one outside this repo).
